say.text: A supine film shows a dilated loop. It sits **centrally**, and its folds run across the full width of the lumen.
Which bowel is dilated?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about where the colon sits on a film, and whether its folds cross the whole width of the lumen.
You may have thought: folds that catch the eye on a busy film must be the colon's, so the loop is large bowel.
That fails because the colon's haustra stay short of the lumen, and this loop is central (K73, K71).
What is right: look at the marker. Valvulae conniventes cross the full width, and that is the small bowel's sign (K6).

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: check the marker before you trust the bowel.

say.text: Yes. The loop is central and its folds cross the full width, so it is small bowel (K71, K6).
Here is one correct read, step by step. **Step 1:** the loops lie centrally, so they are small bowel (K71).
**Step 2:** the folds cross the full width, so they are valvulae conniventes, the small bowel marker (K6).
**Step 3:** small bowel's upper normal is 3 cm, so a 4 cm loop is dilated (K74).
A peer reads the same kind of film and gives three steps. Exactly one step is wrong.
Step 1: the loops are central, so they are small bowel. Step 2: the folds cross the full width, so they are haustra. Step 3: a 4 cm small bowel loop is dilated. Which step is wrong?

choices.label: Step 1: central loops are small bowel
Step 3: a 4 cm small bowel is dilated
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Test each step's marker on its own: does this fold cross the whole lumen, or stop short of it?
You may have swapped the markers in your head: if haustra feel like the small bowel's sign, central loops look like colon.
That fails because valvulae conniventes mark the small bowel, and central loops are small bowel (K71, K6).
What is right: valvulae conniventes cross the full width; haustra stay short of the lumen (K6, K73).

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pin the pairing down: crossing folds go with the small bowel (K6).

say.text: You may have been reaching for 6 cm as the small bowel's limit, because 6 is the number you drill most.
That fails because 6 cm is the colon's upper normal. The small bowel's upper normal is 3 cm (K74).
What is right: the 3-6-9 rule rises as the gut widens. Set the 4 cm loop against its own segment's limit (K74).

sure_note.text: You were sure, so anchor each number to its segment's calibre, not to recall order (K74).

say.text: Yes, that step is the slip. Haustra do not cross the full width; folds that do cross it are valvulae conniventes, the small bowel's marker (K6, K71).
Now the reason. Why is a crossing fold not haustra?

choices.label: Valvulae cross the full width; haustra stop short
Crossing folds are simply bigger haustra
Crossing folds appear only in a dilated colon

say.text: You may be judging by size: a bigger fold looks like a bigger haustrum on a busy film.
That fails because size does not decide the marker. Haustra do not cross the lumen, however large the fold (K73).
What is right: the test is whether the fold crosses the full width, at any calibre (K6).
You may think dilation makes the colon's folds long enough to cross the lumen.
That fails because dilation does not change the marker: haustra stay short of the lumen whatever the calibre (K73).
What is right: a crossing fold marks the small bowel, dilated or not (K6, K71).
Right. The test is whether the fold crosses the full width. Valvulae do; haustra do not (K6).
Which feature is NOT seen in a dilated small bowel loop on a supine film?

choices.label: Folds that cross the full width

say.text: You may have read central loops as colon, so you rule out a central feature for the small bowel.
That fails because a dilated small bowel lies centrally; central is its usual place (K71).
What is right: peripheral loops with short folds are the colon's pattern, so that is the NOT feature (K73).
You may think folds that cross the lumen belong to the colon, so you rule them out of the small bowel.
That fails because crossing valvulae are the small bowel's marker and show in a dilated small bowel (K6).
What is right: the NOT feature is the peripheral one, short folds, which belong to the colon (K73).
Right. A dilated small bowel is central with crossing valvulae; peripheral, short-folded loops are the colon (K71, K73).
On a plain abdominal film, what is the upper normal diameter of the caecum?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about calibre. Which segment is the narrowest, and which is the widest, the caecum or the colon?
You may have reached for 3 cm, the first number of the rule and the narrowest segment you know.
That fails because 3 cm is the small bowel's limit. The caecum is the widest segment, so its number is larger (K74).
What is right: the rule rises as the gut widens, from small bowel to colon to caecum (K74).

sure_note.text: You were sure, so anchor the number to calibre, not to the first number you learned (K74).

say.text: You may have put the caecum in the middle of the rule, because 6 sits in the middle.
That fails because 6 cm is the colon's upper normal, and the caecum is wider than the colon (K74).
What is right: the caecum is the widest segment of the three, so it takes the largest number of the rule (K74).

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the caecum against the colon, not against the middle of the rule (K74).

say.text: Yes. The caecum is the widest segment, at 9 cm. The rule runs 3, 6, 9 down the gut (K74).
Film report: small bowel 4 cm, transverse colon 5 cm, caecum 7 cm. Which segment is dilated?
You may have read the caecum against the small bowel's limit, as if the two shared a number.
That fails because 7 cm sits below the caecum's 9 cm upper normal (K74).
What is right: check each segment against its own limit. Only one of the three is over its own number (K74).
You may have felt the colon is the middle of the rule, so its numbers seem to matter most.
That fails because 5 cm is under the colon's 6 cm upper normal, so the colon is not dilated (K74).
What is right: the 4 cm small bowel loops are the ones over their limit of 3 cm (K74).
You may have assumed a report flags every segment once any number is written down.
That fails because 5 cm and 7 cm sit below their own limits of 6 cm and 9 cm (K74).
What is right: a segment counts as dilated only when it exceeds its own upper normal (K74).
Yes. 4 cm is over the small bowel's 3 cm; 5 cm and 7 cm are under the colon's 6 cm and the caecum's 9 cm (K74).
Plain film: a massively dilated loop arising from the pelvis, shaped like a coffee bean. Which diagnosis?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask where the loop arises: the pelvis, the right side, or the ileocaecal region? Then ask what shape the sign takes.
You may have been tempted because both volvulus types give a big dilated loop, and caecal volvulus is also classic.
That fails because a caecal volvulus gives a kidney-shaped caecum displaced to the left upper quadrant, not a pelvic loop (K77).
What is right: look again at the site and the shape. A pelvic loop with a coffee bean or bent inner tube shape is the clue (K76).

sure_note.text: You were sure, so tie each sign to its site and its disease before you name it (K76, K77).

say.text: You may have been tempted because intussusception is also a classic obstruction that shows as a mass.
That fails because intussusception shows the target, pseudokidney and claw signs, and a coffee bean belongs to a volvulus (K146).
What is right: each sign belongs to one disease and one test. Look at the shape and the site again (K146, K76).

sure_note.text: You were sure, so make a sign card with the disease and the test beside each sign (K146).

say.text: Yes. A pelvic coffee bean or bent inner tube is the sigmoid volvulus sign on plain film (K76, K9).
Which pairing of sign and test is correct?

choices.label: Claw sign on ultrasound; pseudokidney on enema
Claw sign on contrast enema; target on ultrasound
Bird's beak on intussusception enema; target on X-ray
Coffee bean on ultrasound; claw on plain film

say.text: You may be tempted because both signs come from intussusception, so their tests are easy to swap.
That fails because the claw sign is seen on contrast enema, and the pseudokidney on ultrasound (K89, K88).
What is right: keep each sign tied to its test, one test per sign (K89, K88).
You may be tempted because a bird's beak is an enema finding, so any enema sign feels like it fits.
That fails because the bird's beak belongs to sigmoid volvulus on enema, and the target is an ultrasound sign (K87, K88).
What is right: the claw sign marks intussusception on enema, and the target marks it on ultrasound (K89, K88).
You may be tempted because the plain film is the first image, so it seems to carry the first sign.
That fails because the coffee bean is a plain film sign of volvulus, and the claw is an enema sign (K9, K89).
What is right: each sign has its modality. The claw sits on enema, not plain film (K89, K146).
Yes. The claw sign is an enema sign and the target is an ultrasound sign (K89, K88). Keep each sign tied to its test (K146).
An adult with suspected small bowel obstruction. What is the investigation of choice?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which test shows the level, the cause and strangulation together, rather than only that the bowel is blocked.
You may be tempted because the X-ray is the first test ordered, and it does show that the bowel is obstructed.
That fails because the plain film is the initial test. It shows obstruction, not its cause or strangulation (K138).
What is right: ask which test answers the level, the cause and the blood supply together (K7, K81).

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the first test from the definitive one before you choose (K138, K7).

say.text: You may be tempted because a contrast study outlines the bowel and feels like the definitive test.
That fails because barium is unsafe where perforation or large bowel obstruction is possible, and it is not the definitive test (K85, K79).
What is right: a contrast-enhanced CT answers the level, the cause and strangulation at once (K79, K80).

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check safety first: barium is withheld where perforation is possible (K85).

say.text: Yes. Contrast CT answers the level, the cause and strangulation at once (K7, K80). The X-ray only shows that the bowel is blocked (K138).

Match the three questions to their tests in order: the initial test for suspected obstruction, the definitive test for small bowel obstruction, and the diagnostic test for a child with intussusception.

choices.label: Plain film; contrast CT; contrast enema

say.text: You may be tempted because ultrasound is quick and free of radiation, so it feels like the first test everywhere.
That fails because ultrasound is the child's intussusception test, not the start for every obstruction (K137, K138).
What is right: the ladder starts with the plain film, then uses contrast CT for the definitive answer (K138, K79).
You may be tempted because CT is the most informative test, so it seems to belong first.
That fails because the initial test is the plain film, and CT is the definitive test after it (K138, K79).
What is right: for a child with intussusception the diagnostic test is ultrasound, not an enema (K137).
You may be tempted because an enema is the familiar step in an intussusception pathway.
That fails because the child's diagnostic test is ultrasound, the investigation of choice for intussusception (K137, K88).
What is right: keep the question in view. Which test is the diagnostic one for this child, and which is the initial one for any obstruction? (K138, K137)
Yes. The first test for obstruction is the plain film, the definitive test for small bowel obstruction is contrast CT, and a child's intussusception test is ultrasound (K138, K79, K137).
